_metadata.independence: I read only u21-blind-input.json; no other file, search, web lookup or API was consulted.

hints.reason: A glass ball (ornament, crystal ball) for GLASS; the witch gazing into her crystal ball (Wizard of Oz) for WITCH.
Crystal is fine glassware for GLASS; the witch's crystal ball for WITCH.
A mirror is glass (looking glass) for GLASS; the wicked queen-witch's magic mirror in Snow White for WITCH, a step less direct.

best_available.why: Crystal glassware and the witch's crystal ball reach both words at full strength with no story knowledge needed.

pairs.pair_note: All three hints work; CRYSTAL and BALL lean on the same crystal-ball scene, so they are near-variants of each other.

hints.reason: A window is glass for GLASS; nothing recognizable ties a wolf to a window (the fairy-tale wolf comes to the door, not the window).
Wolves howl for WOLF; a howl has no route to glass.

best_available.why: Only because a wolf peering in at grandmother's window is a faintly imaginable scene; it is still one-sided and should not be served as is.

pairs.pair_note: No usable hint. Both candidates are wholly one-sided; the pair needs new candidates (e.g. a shared-fable or shared-object route) before it can run.

hints.reason: Pure gold (24-karat) for GOLD; pure of heart / a pure heart for HEART.
A gold pendant for GOLD; a heart pendant for HEART, the classic heart-shaped gold pendant unites them.
A gold locket for GOLD; the heart-shaped locket for HEART, a single familiar object.

best_available.why: The heart-shaped gold locket is one object that is both words at once.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair; the targets themselves form 'heart of gold'. PENDANT and LOCKET use the same jewellery route.

hints.reason: Amber honey is the standard colour grade for HONEY; amber as a golden hue for GOLD is a shared-colour route like SWEET for APPLE+HONEY.
'Liquid gold' is a familiar phrase (often said of honey itself) for GOLD; honey is a liquid, sold as liquid honey, for HONEY.
Honey drips for HONEY; GOLD is reached only through the idiom 'dripping in gold' or molten gold, a stretch.

best_available.why: Honey is literally called liquid gold, so the hint sits exactly between the two words.

pairs.pair_note: LIQUID is the clear serve; AMBER rides a colour route the rubric allows; DRIP leans heavily on the honey side.

hints.reason: A gold trophy for GOLD; HORSE only via racing trophies, which is a step removed.
A palomino is a horse for HORSE and is defined by its golden coat for GOLD; moderately known (Trigger, Mr. Ed).
Contains the target HORSE as a substring; the lucky gold horseshoe charm would otherwise reach GOLD.

best_available.why: A golden horse by definition; the only hint that reaches both sides cleanly.

pairs.pair_note: HORSESHOE is a rule failure, not a quality failure. PALOMINO's fairness depends on players knowing the breed's colour.

hints.reason: Olympic gold for GOLD; the Winter Olympics' ice events (skating, hockey, curling) for ICE.
Gold medal for GOLD; ICE only through figure-skating medals, a two-step chain.
Ice skating for ICE; GOLD only via winning skating gold, the mirror image of MEDAL's weakness.

best_available.why: Gold medals and ice sports both live inside the Winter Olympics; it is the one hint that reaches both words directly.

pairs.pair_note: MEDAL and SKATING each carry only half the Olympics route; OLYMPICS is the complete one.

hints.reason: Gold ore for GOLD; iron ore for IRON, both everyday compounds.
Fool's gold for GOLD is well known; pyrite being iron sulfide for IRON is correct but needs chemistry knowledge.
Both are metals; a category route that reaches each word plainly.

best_available.why: Gold ore and iron ore are equally familiar compounds, so the hint is balanced and fair.

pairs.pair_note: PYRITE is a clever, factually correct hint whose iron side will be invisible to most players.

hints.reason: Golden ticket (Wonka) for GOLD; no recognizable route to KEY.
City of Gold / El Dorado for GOLD; the key to the city for KEY.
Charlie finds the golden ticket, a two-step route to GOLD; nothing reaches KEY.

best_available.why: Key to the city and City of Gold are both set phrases, giving each side a clear, independent path.

pairs.pair_note: TICKET and CHARLIE are the same Wonka idea and both ignore KEY; only CITY is serviceable.

hints.reason: King Tut for KING; his golden death mask and treasures for GOLD.
King Midas for KING; his golden touch for GOLD, a single famous story.
A gold crown for GOLD; the king's crown for KING.

best_available.why: The golden-touch king is the pair in one name.

pairs.pair_note: Three clean hints; no concerns.

hints.reason: Knights quest for the Holy Grail for KNIGHT; the grail is pictured as a golden chalice for GOLD.
A knight's armor for KNIGHT; golden armor for GOLD is a fantasy image rather than a set association.
Knights 'earn their spurs' for KNIGHT; golden spurs as the badge of knighthood for GOLD is historically right but niche.

best_available.why: The knightly quest and the golden cup are both part of the same familiar legend.

pairs.pair_note: GRAIL is the only hint where the gold side is a recognised image; ARMOR and SPURS reach gold only by colour or history.

hints.reason: Light glows for LIGHT; a golden glow is a stock phrase for GOLD.
Contains the target GOLD; golden light would otherwise be the route to LIGHT.
A halo is a ring of light for LIGHT and is painted gold for GOLD.
Sunset light / golden hour for LIGHT; the golden sunset sky for GOLD.

best_available.why: A halo is simultaneously a light phenomenon and a golden ring.

pairs.pair_note: GOLDEN is a rule failure; the other three are all serviceable, HALO strongest.

hints.reason: Simba is a lion for LION; GOLD only through his golden fur, which no player would name unprompted.
Gold statues (Oscar, idols) for GOLD; lion statues guarding steps and gates for LION.
The lion's mane for LION; a 'golden mane' for GOLD is a colour stretch.

best_available.why: Both words are standard subjects of statues, and a golden lion statue is itself a familiar object.

pairs.pair_note: SIMBA and MANE reach gold only through the lion's colour; STATUE is the one hint with a real gold-side route.

hints.reason: Crescent moon for MOON; a gold crescent for GOLD is a jewellery image at best.
Sun and moon are the classic pairing for MOON; the golden sun for GOLD.
Harvest moon for MOON; golden harvest / harvest gold for GOLD is a colour-phrase stretch.

best_available.why: Sun pairs with moon by habit and with gold by colour and emblem; both routes are instant.

pairs.pair_note: Only SUN reaches gold convincingly; CRESCENT and HARVEST are moon-first hints.

hints.reason: Mickey Mouse for MOUSE; no route to GOLD.
Mice eat cheese for MOUSE; cheese being yellowish is not a recognisable gold route.

best_available.why: Marginally better than MICKEY because golden cheese is at least a visual, but it remains one-sided and should not be served.

pairs.pair_note: No usable hint; both candidates ignore GOLD entirely. The pair needs fresh candidates.

hints.reason: The gold statuette for GOLD; 'Oscar night' for NIGHT.
'Silence is golden' for GOLD; 'Silent Night' for NIGHT, two set phrases reached by ordinary inflection.
Gold stars for GOLD; the night sky's stars for NIGHT.

best_available.why: Gold star and night stars are both immediate for any player.

pairs.pair_note: Three good hints with three different routes; SILENCE is the most elegant, STARS the broadest.

hints.reason: Spanish galleons carried gold for GOLD and sailed the ocean for OCEAN.
Shipwreck gold / treasure for GOLD; wrecks lie in the ocean for OCEAN.
Sunken treasure / gold for GOLD; sunken in the ocean for OCEAN.

best_available.why: The sunken-treasure scene is universally known and names both words at once.

pairs.pair_note: All three draw on the same treasure-ship scene; SHIPWRECK is the broadest version.

hints.reason: Golden Jubilee for GOLD; the Queen's Jubilee for QUEEN, widely covered beyond the UK.
A golden throne for GOLD; the queen on her throne for QUEEN.
A gold crown for GOLD; a queen's crown for QUEEN.

best_available.why: Gold crown and queen's crown are the first associations for both words.

pairs.pair_note: Clean pair; JUBILEE is the most specific and slightly UK-leaning but still well known.

hints.reason: C-3PO is a golden robot: the spelled-out nickname reaches both GOLD and ROBOT, though the spelling is less instantly read than C3PO.
Gold-plated for GOLD; a robot's metal plating for ROBOT is a weaker, descriptive route.
The golden Star Wars droid is both GOLD and ROBOT in one name.

best_available.why: The most recognised golden robot in popular culture.

pairs.pair_note: C3PO and THREEPIO are the same hint in two spellings; serve one.

hints.reason: A gold vein for GOLD; veins run through rock for ROCK.
Prospectors hunt gold for GOLD; they pick through rock for ROCK, a recognisable scene.
Gold ore for GOLD; ore is metal-bearing rock for ROCK.
Gold nugget for GOLD; a nugget is a small lump of rock for ROCK.

best_available.why: Ore is literally gold-bearing rock, so neither side is a stretch.

pairs.pair_note: A strong mining pair; all four hints share one scene but each reaches both words.

hints.reason: Gilded means gold-coated for GOLD; a gilded rose (gold-dipped gift rose) for ROSE is a product, not a set association.
Rose is a shade of pink for ROSE; pink gold is the other name for rose gold for GOLD.
The gold and rose-gold iPhone finishes make the brand reach both GOLD and ROSE, as Apple does for APPLE+CARD.

best_available.why: Pink is the colour of a rose and the literal description of rose/pink gold.

pairs.pair_note: The targets form 'rose gold'; PINK and IPHONE both lean on that compound, GILDED leans only on gold.

hints.reason: Gold flakes (leaf, Goldschlager) for GOLD; flaky sea salt for SALT.
'Worth its weight in gold' for GOLD; 'worth one's salt' for SALT, two idioms.
Gold mine for GOLD; salt mine for SALT.

best_available.why: Gold mine and salt mine are equally common compounds.

pairs.pair_note: Three good hints; WORTH is the most satisfying idiom-based route.

hints.reason: Gold glints for GOLD; a glint has no route to SHADOW.
Gold shimmers for GOLD; nothing reaches SHADOW.
Contains the target SHADOW; gold eyeshadow would otherwise reach both words.

best_available.why: Nothing here is serviceable; GLINT is named only because it is a valid gold-side word, and it should not be served.

pairs.pair_note: No usable hint. EYESHADOW shows the intended route (makeup) but breaks the substring rule; a hint like a makeup brand or 'LID' would need testing instead.

hints.reason: Loan shark for SHARK; a gold loan (gold as collateral) for GOLD is regionally familiar but faint for most players.
A gold tooth for GOLD; a shark tooth for SHARK.

best_available.why: Gold tooth and shark tooth are both instant compounds.

pairs.pair_note: TOOTH carries the pair alone; LOAN is a shark-first hint.

hints.reason: A gold bracelet for GOLD; the coiled snake bracelet / armband for SNAKE, a recognised jewellery design.
Gold chain for GOLD; snake chain is a jewellery chain style, and a chain is snake-like, for SNAKE.
The serpent house for SNAKE; Slytherin's colours are green and silver, not gold (gold belongs to Gryffindor), so the GOLD side is a wrong fact.

best_available.why: The gold snake bracelet is a single familiar object.

pairs.pair_note: SLYTHERIN is a factual miss; BRACELET and CHAIN both work through jewellery.

hints.reason: Orb-weaver spiders for SPIDER; the golden orb of royal regalia (and the golden orb-weaver) for GOLD; both sides require specialist knowledge.
Spider silk for SPIDER; gold silk is a fabric colour for GOLD, a stretch.

best_available.why: Spider silk is immediate and gold silk is at least a recognisable material, making it the fairer of two stretches.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. Both hints hover around the golden orb-weaver spider, which few players know; the pair wants a new angle.

hints.reason: Pot of gold for GOLD; no route to SPRING.
Forsythia is an early-spring shrub for SPRING; its yellow-gold blossom for GOLD is a colour route few players will know.
The daffodil is the spring flower for SPRING; 'golden daffodils' (Wordsworth) for GOLD is a colour phrase.

best_available.why: Daffodil is instant for spring and 'golden daffodils' is a well-worn phrase, so it is the least one-sided candidate.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. The two flower hints reach gold only by colour; POT ignores spring entirely.

hints.reason: The Christmas tree's star topper for STAR and gold tinsel for GOLD; a shared scene, but neither link is direct from the bare word TREE.
The gold star sticker is one object that is both GOLD and STAR.
The sheriff's badge is a gold star: STAR by shape, GOLD by metal.

best_available.why: Everyone has seen a gold star sticker; it is the compound itself.

pairs.pair_note: STICKER and SHERIFF are both good; TREE needs the Christmas scene to be supplied by the player.

hints.reason: Railroad spike for TRAIN; the Golden Spike that completed the transcontinental railroad for GOLD, well known in the US.
Gold rush for GOLD; rush-hour trains for TRAIN is a loose association.
The Great Train Robbery / Wild West train robbery for TRAIN; the gold shipment being robbed for GOLD, a recognised scene.

best_available.why: Rail spike and Golden Spike reach both words through one piece of railway history.

pairs.pair_note: SPIKE's gold side is US-history knowledge; ROBBERY is broader but gold is one of several things trains carry.

hints.reason: Gold panned from rivers for GOLD; a river is water for WATER.
Panning for gold for GOLD; the pan is swirled in water (and a pan of water is everyday) for WATER.
Contains the target GOLD; the fish in water would otherwise reach WATER.

best_available.why: The gold-in-the-river scene is familiar and the water side is literal.

pairs.pair_note: GOLDFISH is a rule failure; RIVER and PAN share the prospecting scene.

hints.reason: Alchemists sought to make gold for GOLD; alchemy as a sister art to witchcraft (potions, magic) for WITCH.
Glinda the Good Witch for WITCH; nothing about her reaches GOLD.
The witch's cauldron for WITCH; the leprechaun's pot is not usually called a cauldron, so GOLD is not reached.

best_available.why: Only hint with a gold-side route; the witch side is a reasonable magic-arts leap.

pairs.pair_note: ALCHEMY carries the pair; GLINDA and CAULDRON are witch-only filler.

hints.reason: Wolves' golden/amber eyes are the shared property, but EYES alone points at neither GOLD nor WOLF without that specific image.
Streets paved with gold for GOLD; The Wolf of Wall Street for WOLF.

best_available.why: Two set phrases, one per side, with no factual stretch.

pairs.pair_note: STREET is the serve; EYES is a shared-property route that is too diffuse to land.

hints.reason: The heart is the symbol of love for HEART; honey is a term of endearment, like love, for HONEY.
Darling and honey are sibling endearments for HONEY; HEART is reached only via 'sweetheart' or 'dear heart', a step away.
Sweetheart for HEART; honey is sweet for HONEY.

best_available.why: Sweetheart and sweet honey are both instant.

pairs.pair_note: SWEET and LOVE are strong; DARLING is honey-first.

hints.reason: Heartbeat for HEART; 'beating a dead horse' and the beat of hooves for HORSE.
A racing heart for HEART; horse race for HORSE.
Horses gallop for HORSE; a 'galloping heart' for HEART is literary and less common than 'racing'.

best_available.why: Heart race and horse race are equally everyday.

pairs.pair_note: RACE is the clean serve; BEAT works via idiom; GALLOP is RACE's weaker cousin.

hints.reason: A frozen heart (and the film's plot) for HEART; frozen water is ice for ICE.
Elsa's ice powers for ICE; HEART only via her freezing Anna's heart, a plot point rather than an instant association.
Cold-hearted for HEART; ice is cold for ICE.

best_available.why: Frozen heart and frozen ice are both immediate, and the Disney film reinforces the pairing.

pairs.pair_note: FROZEN and COLD are solid; ELSA is a judgement call that could rise to PASS if the Frozen plot counts as a familiar story like Snow White.

hints.reason: Keychain for KEY; a heart on a chain (necklace) for HEART.
A key unlocks for KEY; unlocking someone's heart / 'key to my heart' for HEART.
A heart locket for HEART; KEY only via 'key to my heart' locket designs or the 'lock' inside the word, not a set association.

best_available.why: The 'key to my heart' idea makes unlock reach both words at full strength.

pairs.pair_note: UNLOCK is excellent; LOCKET is heart-first.

hints.reason: King Richard for KING; Richard the Lionheart for HEART, a compound counting as the compound.
The king card and the hearts suit (king of hearts) for KING and HEART.
Contains the target HEART; otherwise the same route as RICHARD.

best_available.why: The king of hearts is a single card that is both words.

pairs.pair_note: LIONHEART is a rule failure; RICHARD delivers the same idea legally.

hints.reason: Chivalry is the knightly code for KNIGHT; HEART only through courtly romance, a diffuse link.
Braveheart / a brave heart for HEART; a brave knight for KNIGHT.
The knight's lady for KNIGHT; HEART only via the lady who holds his heart, which needs the courtly-love frame.

best_available.why: Brave heart and brave knight are both stock phrases.

pairs.pair_note: BRAVE carries the pair; CHIVALRY and LADY are knight-first with a romance stretch to heart.

hints.reason: A heavy heart for HEART; heavy is the opposite of light for LIGHT.
Light as a feather for LIGHT; HEART only via the Egyptian weighing of the heart against a feather, which is niche.

best_available.why: The idiom and the antonym are both instant.

pairs.pair_note: HEAVY is a good serve; the pair itself also reads as 'light heart'. FEATHER is light-first.

hints.reason: Heart means courage ('take heart') for HEART; the Cowardly Lion seeking courage for LION.
Braveheart / brave heart for HEART; the brave lion for LION.
Richard the Lionheart reaches LION and HEART through one epithet.

best_available.why: The Wizard of Oz gives the lion courage and the shared meaning of heart as courage closes the loop.

pairs.pair_note: Three clean hints; the pair is 'lionheart' itself.

hints.reason: A full heart for HEART; a full moon for MOON.
The heart as love's symbol for HEART; the moon as the romantic emblem ('to the moon and back') for MOON.
To pine is a heart's yearning for HEART; 'to moon over' someone is a synonym of pine for MOON, a verb route too clever to land.

best_available.why: Full moon and full heart are both set phrases.

pairs.pair_note: FULL is the serve; LOVE is a fair romance route; PINE relies on the rare verb sense of moon.
